Hi Aaron — great to speak earlier. Quick written recap so we have alignment and a clear path to the next technical dive. I pulled together the items we discussed and what we need to qualify Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private VPC/On‑Prem for Catalyst Health.

Summary of what you said:
- Primary goal: low-latency inference for real‑time clinician assistant (95th p99 target ~200ms on short prompts).
- Data sensitivity: PHI in prompts, so you need strong KMS integration and audit logs.
- Cost target: prefer predictable monthly for peak loads (can consider reserved Dedicated).
- Risk tolerance: cannot have noisy-neighbor incidents that increase tail latency during business hours.

Qualification checklist (items we promised to follow up on):
1) Performance/SLOs — confirm typical qps and peak burst windows; which endpoints require p99 SLAs.
2) Isolation needs — are shared-hosted tiers acceptable for non-prod, or must production be dedicated from day one?
3) Networking & data flow — inbound/outbound connectivity, VPC peering, private link preferences.
4) Compliance evidence — SOC 2, encryption at rest/in transit, key management requirements.
5) Procurement timeline — lead times for Dedicated contracts and any procurement docs.

Attachments: I attached a blank Mutual Action Plan template for us to iterate (Catalyst_MutualActionPlan_v1.pdf) and the security questionnaire we usually receive (SOC2-Questions.xlsx).

Next steps I propose:
- Sean to run a short technical note on noisy-neighbor mitigations and what Dedicated buys you vs tuning Hosted (by Mon, Jun 1).
- Schedule a 60-min technical deep-dive with your infra/security folks and our infra lead (propose Wed Jun 3 or Thu Jun 4).

Kimberly — thanks for the clear recap. This aligns well. A few clarifications from our side:

1) SLOs: clinician-facing assistant must hit p95 < 120ms and p99 < 300ms for short, structured prompts during peak (8am-6pm PT). Non‑clinical background tasks can tolerate higher tails.
2) Isolation: for initial pilot (100 clinicians) we are comfortable with a dedicated capacity rather than full on‑prem. Production (scale rollout) may require Private VPC or on‑prem options depending on legal review.
3) Noisy neighbor: this is a hard requirement — any single‑tenant/dedicated offering should include documented isolation boundaries and a remediation SLA if tail latency exceeds thresholds.
4) Compliance: we will want to review SOC 2 Type II evidence, encryption key management options (bring your own key), and the audit log retention policy.

Procurement: I looped in procurement@catalysthealth.com. Our procurement lead will need a draft SOW and estimated monthly committed cost for Dedicated plus an option for Private VPC pricing.

Aaron / Kimberly — quick technical note on isolation and noisy-neighbor mitigations for Catalyst’s use-case. High level points only; we can expand in the deep-dive.

1) What Dedicated gives you vs Hosted (practical differences)
- Dedicated capacity: reserved GPU pool dedicated to your tenant; predictable throughput and isolated process-level resources. Good for predictable p99 behavior and cost forecasting.
- Hosted (shared): runs on multi-tenant pools with soft isolation; benefits are lower cost and instant scaling, but rare noisy-neighbor events can increase tail latency unless mitigated.

2) Isolation boundaries and guarantees
- Dedicated: single-tenant job queues + isolated worker groups; KV cache namespaces are tenant-scoped. We can offer explicit CPU/GPU allocation policies and quota caps per worker to reduce cross-tenant interference.
- Private VPC/On‑prem: full network and control-plane separation; customer-managed keys (BYOK) and direct peering for lowest cross-network variability.

3) SLO instrumentation and remediation
- We instrument token-level latency, per-node p99s, and request traces. For Dedicated customers we offer per-route p99 dashboards and a 24/7 escalation channel.
- Remediation policy example: if p99 exceeds agreed threshold for >5 min during business hours, we auto‑trigger traffic migration to a warm standby or increase dedicated capacity and issue incident credits per SLA.

4) Practical mitigations that don’t require Dedicated day‑one
- Request‑level QoS and priority lanes for clinical routes (higher scheduling priority).
- Prefix/KV caching for common prompts to reduce inference work at tail.
- Pre-provisioned burst capacity for known peak windows.

5) Network & security notes
- For Private/VPC we support AWS VPC peering and PrivateLink. KMS integrations support AWS KMS and external HSM via standard APIs (we will need the KMS ARN and key management policy).

Attachments: short table (not included here) with latency budgets and sample capacity configs. Happy to put formal config examples in the deep-dive.
